I'm 17, in the UK and I need a job. pls help.
Newly employed people of Voat, how did you do it, and what are your top tips?
Give some background. What field are you looking at? What are your basic qualifications: degrees / experience. Without that I can't help much. Different situations call for different strategies.

I've been in charge of hiring in a number of different positions over the years. Although this is was in the United States, and different countries may have different customs, I'm pretty sure these are universal enough.

Have somebody review your resume: Even the best writers have editors, and it's for a reason. You spend enough time looking at the same thing all day, you're going to miss mistakes. I would toss out any resume that had a spelling error on it. I have too many resumes and not enough jobs. Just to be considered, I expect this to be perfect.

Sometime it's who you know: If you apply for a job, find out who in your social network already works there. It could be a second cousin of a friend you never see anymore. Just find somebody. Take the time to call them up and find out some details about the company, and see if they can help you out. Dropping a name during an interview will increase your chances, and may even make you a shoo-in.

Be persistent in getting an interview: Once again, there are more applicants than jobs and I can only interview so many people during the day. I like the person who called me up three or four times asking me for a chance to interview. It shows that they want the job, and that they follow up on things...and that last bit helps to determine who is going to be a good employee down the road. If you put in a resume, do at least two follow up calls.

Be prepared for the interview: Show up ten minutes early. Have a pen with you. Be dressed one notch up from the people who work the job you're applying to. If they wear polo shirts, you wear a dress shirt and tie. If they wear dress shirts, you wear a suit. Know who it is you're going to see, and use their name when you talk to them. When I ask you "do you have any questions for us?" be sure to answer with some questions that show you have a understanding of who we are and what you'll be expected to do.

Send a thank you letter: The interview doesn't end when you get home. I might have four or five people I liked just as much as you. If you send me a card or a letter, it might help to push me in your direction.

Good luck in finding a job!
Like a physical letter/card or email? Thanks for the very informative answer!

Physical is best. Not just because people who hire are old bastards like me, but because it sits on the desk as a reminder. An e-mail can be ignored, a physical letter or card can't. As soon as you get home from the interview, write something nice and mail it out. Most of the time they'll get it the next morning and be a bit impressed. I would get a "thank you for the interview and the opportunity" letter for one or two out of every twenty people I interviewed. They racked up some points for it, that's for sure.
So should I type it out? Or should I just end up buying a 'Thank You' card and say something like, "Thanks for the Interview and I hope to hear from you soon!" kind of thing?

Play to your strengths, and base it on the person you interviewed with. I'm a pretty solid writer when someone is paying me, so I tend to type out a nice letter. It gives me a chance to self promote a bit ("It was very exciting have the opportunity to talk with you about the position. It's rare I have a chance to interview for a job that seems so well suited for me...etc, etc.). I can backfire if the tone is read wrong, however.

Cards are good, and should be done by hand, hitting the same main points. At least three sentences.

I manage my online presence very intensely. I ended up with my current job because someone saw who I was and what I was doing, and wanted to hire me.

In the past, I have had very good luck in finding employment due to what I think are the following reasons:

1) I deliver my resume and cover letter (both carefully tailored to the company) to the location, asking to see whoever is in charge of hiring. Have a wide variety of references on that resume that will actually pick up the phone if an unknown number calls them. My biggest jump in employment was when I had my manager's assistant pretend to be the manager and vouch for me because the actual manager was a total douchebag and deliberately sabotages people's efforts to leave. Really consider every aspect of what you're presenting to the employer.

2) I dress very conservatively and nicely. No jewelry, but well-kempt hair and new-looking clothes

3) During the interview, I maintain a happy demeanor but approach the interview kind of like a date. Even if I'm desperate, I act like working for them is a choice I need to explore before making a decision. Doing so makes the employer feel that you are really considering a long-term situation and usually agree with you if you decide it would be a good fit (after asking lots of questions, getting a walk-through of the work area, and meeting coworkers). Avoid self-depreciating and mentioning anything in your personal life.

4) I follow up with a thank-you email, telling them I appreciate their time and wish them the best in their business ventures

Edit: Also, never underestimate the power of scent. For a high-volume work environment, I'll wear mint or citrus. If it's going to be relaxed and service-focused, I wear lavender. If seeming sexy will give me an advantage, I wear amber. The trick is to wear very little - a splash on the wrists and nothing more.

This is a petty quibble, but it's annoying when Dimetrodon is depicted as a dinosaur, or alongside dinosaurs. They're pelycosaurs, a type of synapsid. While they are not ancestral to mammals, or the direct ancestors of extant mammals, they're actually phylogenetically closer to mammals than to the Dinosauria, which are Diapsids. The divergence between synapsid and diapsid animals happened very early during the evolution of reptiles, so Dimetrodon has nothing to do with dinosaurs.
